stem: A security architect asks where the web application, job scheduler and notebook service of a Databricks workspace run, compared with the place where Spark processes the data of a classic compute cluster. Which description is correct?

choices.text: Both the web application and classic compute run in the control plane, and the customer's cloud account only stores the cloud audit logs of the workspace
The web application and scheduling services run in the control plane managed by Databricks; classic compute runs in the compute plane inside the customer's own cloud account
The web application and scheduling services run in the customer's cloud account; classic compute runs in a compute plane that Databricks operates in its own account
Both the web application and classic compute run in the customer's cloud account, and Databricks supplies only the Spark runtime images used by the clusters

stem: A nightly job runs `INSERT INTO sales_silver SELECT * FROM staging_sales` on a Delta table. The cluster is terminated by an out-of-memory error after the write has produced some data files but before the job finished. What does a reader querying `sales_silver` see afterwards?

choices.text: An error on every query until someone runs `VACUUM`, since the orphaned files make the table state inconsistent for readers
The partial rows from the files written before the failure, because Delta appends each data file to the table as soon as it is written
Only the rows from the first half of the job, since Delta rolls back the failed commit but keeps the files that were completed
The table in its state before the failed job, because the files are added to the table only when the transaction log commit succeeds

stem: A data engineer ran `DELETE FROM orders WHERE region = 'EU'` on a Delta table by mistake. Yesterday's table state is needed for a report, and no `VACUUM` has been run. Which statement lets the engineer find the version before the delete and read it?

choices.text: `DESCRIBE DETAIL orders`, which lists every earlier table version and can be queried directly for the rows of each version
`SELECT * FROM orders@v-1`, because the table name suffix always returns the previous version regardless of later changes
`DESCRIBE HISTORY orders`, then `SELECT * FROM orders VERSION AS OF <version before the DELETE>` with the number found in the history
`SELECT * FROM orders VERSION AS OF 0`, because version 0 is always the state of the table before the latest operation

stem: A pipeline run replaced the contents of a Delta table with bad data. The table history shows the last good state as version 41, and the files for that version are still within the retention period. The engineer wants the table itself, not just a query, to return to that state. Which command does that?

choices.text: `RESTORE TABLE customers TO VERSION AS OF 41`, which requires MODIFY permission and creates a new commit that reverts the table's contents
`VACUUM customers RETAIN 0 HOURS`, which deletes data files from versions newer than the one named by the retention setting
`CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE customers SHALLOW CLONE customers`, which rolls back the table by cloning the current version again
`DELETE FROM customers VERSION AS OF 41`, which removes every row that was added to the table after that version

stem: Last month a table was changed several times. Today `SELECT * FROM events TIMESTAMP AS OF '2026-10-01'` fails because the files are gone, although the table history still lists that date. A weekly `VACUUM` runs with default settings and the table properties were never changed. What explains this?

choices.text: `OPTIMIZE` rewrote the table into larger files, which deletes the older versions of the table from the transaction log at the same moment
Time travel is limited to the last 24 hours, so any older timestamp always fails regardless of the table properties and of the maintenance that runs
Time travel needs the table to be a managed table, and the older versions of an external table are never readable after thirty days
Table history and time travel use different thresholds: the history is kept longer, while data files are removed by `VACUUM` once they pass the file retention

stem: A team creates a table with `CREATE TABLE main.sales.orders (id BIGINT, amount DECIMAL(10,2))` and no `USING` clause in a Unity Catalog enabled workspace. In which storage format is the table created?

choices.text: Parquet, because it is the open file format that Spark uses when a table definition does not name any other format
Delta Lake, because it is the default table format on Databricks when the format is not specified
CSV, because the schema contains only simple types and Spark writes a delimited text file when no format is named
Apache Iceberg, because Unity Catalog managed tables use that format whenever the statement omits the format clause

stem: In a workspace that uses Unity Catalog, an engineer wants to query the table `customers` that belongs to the schema `crm` of the catalog `prod`. Which reference follows the Unity Catalog object model?

choices.text: `SELECT * FROM prod.customers.crm`, since the table name sits between the catalog and the schema
`SELECT * FROM metastore.prod.crm.customers`, using the metastore name as an extra prefix before the catalog
`SELECT * FROM prod.crm.customers`, using the three-level namespace catalog, schema and table
`SELECT * FROM crm.prod.customers`, since the schema is always named first and the catalog second

stem: A company runs five Databricks workspaces for different teams and needs one place to define who can read which tables, to see lineage and to audit access, regardless of the workspace used. Which platform component provides this?

choices.text: Unity Catalog, the governance layer that provides centralized access control, lineage, auditing and data discovery across workspaces
Delta Lake's transaction log, which records the grants of every user together with the data files of each table
Cluster access modes set on the compute of each team, which apply one common permission model to every workspace
The Hive metastore of each workspace, which stores table definitions locally and is shared automatically with every other workspace

stem: A nightly ETL notebook runs on an all-purpose cluster that three engineers also use for ad hoc work. The cluster is idle most of the day, and the team wants to lower cost without changing the code. Which change fits best?

choices.text: Move the notebook to a SQL warehouse, which is the compute that Databricks designed for scheduled Python data engineering code
Turn off autoscaling on the all-purpose cluster and set a fixed number of workers, which stops the cluster from paying for idle time
Run the notebook as a Lakeflow Jobs task on job compute, or serverless compute for jobs, so resources exist only while the run lasts
Keep the all-purpose cluster running all day with a larger node type, so the nightly run finishes sooner and ends before the day begins

stem: Business analysts run dashboards and ad hoc SQL queries against gold tables all day with changing concurrency. The platform team wants minimal administration and quick start-up with no clusters to size. Which compute should serve these queries?

choices.text: A cluster with the Spark RDD API enabled, as it is the interface that dashboards use to read gold tables
A serverless SQL warehouse, which Databricks recommends where available for SQL and BI workloads
A classic jobs cluster that a scheduled job starts every morning and terminates in the evening
A single-node all-purpose cluster with the largest instance type, shared by all analysts through a notebook

stem: An engineer prototypes with a 5 MB CSV file and a single-threaded Python library that does not use Spark executors. A multi-node cluster would be mostly idle. Which classic compute configuration is intended for this?

choices.text: A single node compute resource, which runs Spark locally for small data or non-distributed workloads
A multi-node cluster with a high minimum worker count, to leave room for scaling when the file gets larger
A SQL warehouse of the smallest size, because it runs Python libraries that do not depend on Spark
A pool of idle instances used as the driver, which avoids having any worker nodes in the compute

stem: A notebook that uses `sc.parallelize(data).map(f).collect()` runs on a classic cluster but fails on serverless compute for notebooks with an error about unsupported operations. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: Serverless compute disables Delta Lake access, so a notebook that reads tables must be moved back to classic compute
Serverless compute runs only SQL statements, so any notebook cell written in Python is rejected before the notebook starts running
Serverless compute has no driver node, so any code that collects results to the driver fails with an error about memory
Serverless compute supports only Spark Connect APIs, and the Spark RDD API used by the code is not supported

stem: A data scientist develops notebooks interactively for a few hours a day and often forgets to stop the classic all-purpose cluster, which runs overnight. Which setting reduces the cost of this idle time without changing the workflow?

choices.text: A Databricks Runtime LTS version, whose cluster stops by itself when no notebook is attached to it
A higher maximum number of workers, so that queries use more nodes and finish before the user is away
An auto termination period, so the cluster shuts down after the chosen number of minutes of inactivity
A larger driver node, so that the notebook finishes its commands faster and the cluster is released earlier

stem: A team compares compute for a transformation written in SQL and PySpark that runs hourly as a Lakeflow Jobs notebook task with unpredictable data volume. They do not want to size clusters or manage the runtime. Which option matches?

choices.text: Serverless compute for jobs, because Databricks provisions and scales the resources automatically for each run
A single-node cluster that a person starts by hand before each run, so that the data volume is always known
An all-purpose cluster with a fixed number of workers, since it is the only compute type that jobs can use
A Pro SQL warehouse, because it is the compute for PySpark notebook tasks of Lakeflow Jobs

stem: Three engineers work on the same repository and each wants to develop notebooks in the Databricks workspace without overwriting each other. Which workflow follows the recommended practice for Databricks Git folders?

choices.text: One engineer owns a Git folder, and the others write notebooks in plain workspace folders that the owner copies into the repository
All three edit the same Git folder under a shared workspace folder and commit to the main branch directly after each change
Each engineer exports notebooks as files, edits them locally and uploads them to the workspace to replace the version in the Git folder
Each engineer clones the repository into their own Git folder, works on a personal branch and merges by pull request on the Git provider

stem: Two engineers use the same shared Git folder. After one of them switched the folder to a different branch, the other found notebooks suddenly showing different code. How should the team avoid this?

choices.text: Disable the pull operation in the shared folder so the notebooks never change after the first clone of the repository
Give each engineer their own Git folder cloned from the remote, with Git operations done only by its owner
Create more branches in the shared Git folder and ask engineers to remember to switch back before they edit
Lock the shared folder so that only workspace admins may edit it, and ask engineers to send code in a ticket

stem: A team wants workspace jobs to run notebooks from the reviewed `release` branch only. Developers must not edit that code in the workspace, and updates should appear automatically after a pull request is merged. Which setup fits?

choices.text: A user-level Git folder for every developer under the user home path, all of them switched to the release branch
A Git folder with Can Edit permission for all users so anyone can pull the release branch whenever needed
A workspace folder where developers paste the final notebooks after approval and then mark them read-only
A production Git folder created by an admin on the release branch, run-only for users, updated by automation after merges

stem: An engineer cannot clone a very large repository into a Git folder because the operation fails with a size error, although the notebooks needed are in only two directories. What is the recommended approach?

choices.text: Configure sparse checkout mode when creating the Git folder so that only the needed directories are cloned
Split the clone into two Git folders by cloning the same repository twice and deleting half of the files in each
Grant the engineer CAN MANAGE on the parent folder, which removes the size limits for clones by that user
Clone with the default branch only and then rebase on the first commit of the repository to shrink the history

stem: An engineer finished a change in a Git folder but the Git provider rejects pushes to the protected default branch, and the engineer has no permission to commit there. What should the engineer do in the Git folder workflow?

choices.text: Delete the Git folder and clone again, which grants the engineer the commit rights of the repository owner
Commit to a new branch, push it, and create a pull request on the Git provider to merge it into the default branch
Edit the file directly on the default branch in the provider's web page and pull it back into the folder
Force the push to the default branch with the hard reset option of the branch menu so the provider accepts it

stem: A bundle deploys a job that writes to a schema. The schema must be `etl_dev` for the `dev` target and `etl_prod` for `prod`, with `dev` as the default. The team wants one job definition, not two. Which approach follows the bundle configuration model?

choices.text: Declare the schema name as a Python constant in each notebook and edit the notebook after each deployment
Copy the bundle folder into two projects, one per environment, and replace the schema name in the job file of each copy
Declare a variable `schema_name` with a default, reference it as `${var.schema_name}`, and set `variables` for the `prod` target
Use the `${bundle.environment}` substitution with a different value in each cloud account, set from the workspace settings

stem: A bundle declares `variables: {warehouse_size: {default: Small}}` and the `prod` target sets `warehouse_size: Large` under its `variables`. A CI pipeline runs `databricks bundle validate -t prod --var="warehouse_size=Medium"` with `BUNDLE_VAR_warehouse_size=XL` also set. Which value does the CLI use?

choices.text: XL, because environment variables take precedence over every other source of values
Large, because the value written in the target's configuration is the most specific
Medium, because the `--var` option is checked first, before environment variables and target values
Small, because the default is the only value that can pass validation

stem: A bundle sets the variable `input_path` to a different value in each deployment. After deployment, the engineer starts the job from the Jobs UI with a new value for `input_path` as a bundle variable, but the run still uses the deployed value. Why?

choices.text: Bundle variables are only read from the `default` setting, so the targets mapping cannot change their value
The variable must have type `complex` to be changed after deployment, and plain string variables are fixed forever
The Jobs UI always uses the value of the `dev` target, whatever target was used for the last deployment
Bundle variables are resolved at deployment time, so per-run values must be supplied through job parameters instead

stem: A job defined at the top level of a bundle has a job cluster with `job_cluster_key: main` and 2 workers. The `prod` target should use 8 workers on the same cluster, keeping every other setting. How is this expressed?

choices.text: Set `num_workers` in the top-level `variables` mapping, which automatically changes the job cluster for the last-deployed target
Put `num_workers: 8` under a job_clusters entry with `job_cluster_key: main` in the `prod` target's job resource, which overrides that setting
Redefine the whole `resources` block under `prod`, since a target replaces the top-level resources and nothing is merged
Declare a second job named like the first in the `prod` target, which then runs next to the original job after deployment

stem: A bundle job runs a SQL task on a warehouse named `Shared Analytics`. The warehouse ID differs in each workspace, and the team does not want IDs in the files. Which feature supplies the right ID per workspace?

choices.text: A variable with a `lookup` for the `warehouse` object type, which resolves the ID of the warehouse with that name
A job parameter named `warehouse_id` that the scheduler fills in with the first warehouse found in the workspace
A Git folder variable that stores the warehouse ID, which the Git provider replaces during every push
A hardcoded ID in the top-level job definition, edited through a pull request each time the workspace changes

stem: A nightly job reads a bronze table where every column was ingested as STRING and writes a typed silver table with `CAST(quantity AS INT)`. The job now fails with a CAST_INVALID_INPUT error because a few rows contain values such as `N/A` and `12x`. The team wants the job to keep running and wants the unparseable values to become NULL so they can be reviewed. Which change fits?

choices.text: Wrap the existing cast in `coalesce(CAST(quantity AS INT), 0)`, which catches the error and substitutes zero for bad rows
Add `nullif(quantity, 'N/A')` around the existing cast, which removes every invalid value the source can ever contain
Replace `CAST(quantity AS INT)` with `CAST(quantity AS DOUBLE)`, which accepts any text and returns 0.0 for values that cannot be converted
Replace `CAST(quantity AS INT)` with `try_cast(quantity AS INT)`, which returns NULL for values that cannot be converted

stem: In a silver table, the `country` column should never be NULL for downstream reports. Rows from one source system arrive with a NULL country, and the business agreed that these rows should show the label `UNKNOWN`. All other values must stay unchanged. Which expression does this?

choices.text: `coalesce(country, 'UNKNOWN')`, which returns country when it is not NULL and the label `UNKNOWN` otherwise
`nullif(country, 'UNKNOWN')`, which returns the label for rows where country is NULL and leaves other values unchanged
`country <=> 'UNKNOWN'`, which returns the label for rows where country is NULL and the original value elsewhere
`isnull(country)`, which returns the label for rows where country is NULL and the original value elsewhere

stem: A CSV source writes a missing e-mail address as an empty string or as spaces (`''` or `'   '`), and the silver table should store a real NULL instead so that `email IS NULL` finds all missing values. Which expression produces that result for a column named `email`?

choices.text: `trim(nullif(email, ''))`, which turns only exactly-empty strings into NULL before trimming
`nullif(trim(email), '')`, which trims the text first and then returns NULL when what remains is empty
`regexp_replace(email, ' ', '')`, which removes spaces and turns blank values into NULL automatically
`coalesce(trim(email), '')`, which returns an empty string when the e-mail is blank or NULL

stem: An analyst builds a silver view with `SELECT * FROM bronze.tickets WHERE status <> 'CLOSED'` to list open work. Operations reports that tickets with no status value are missing from the result, although they should count as open. What explains this, and what is the fix?

choices.text: `<>` is case sensitive, so the tickets are lost when status is `closed`; wrap the column in `lower()` and compare with `'closed'`
`<>` is not supported for strings in a WHERE clause; replace it with `NOT LIKE 'CLOSED'` to keep every unmatched row
Comparisons with NULL evaluate to unknown, so those rows are filtered out; use `status IS DISTINCT FROM 'CLOSED'`
Rows with NULL are always removed by SELECT *; replace the star with an explicit column list to keep them

stem: A bronze table stores event times as strings. Source A writes `2026-03-14 08:30:00`, source B writes `03/14/2026`, and some rows hold text such as `unknown`. The silver table needs a TIMESTAMP column that is NULL for anything that matches neither pattern, without the job failing. Which expression fits?

choices.text: `to_timestamp(ts)`, which raises no error for the second pattern and rejects `unknown` rows into a quarantine location automatically
`try_to_timestamp(ts, 'yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss')`, which also parses the slash pattern because the format is only a hint
`coalesce(try_to_timestamp(ts, 'yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss'), try_to_timestamp(ts, 'MM/dd/yyyy'))`
`cast(ts AS DATE)`, which accepts both patterns and returns a date at midnight for the text values

stem: A PySpark job loads a bronze DataFrame `df`. Business rules say a row is unusable if either `order_id` or `customer_id` is NULL, but NULLs in other columns are acceptable. Which statement removes exactly the unusable rows?

choices.text: `df.na.drop()`, which drops a row when the two named columns are NULL and ignores the others
`df.dropna(subset=["order_id", "customer_id"])`, which drops a row when either column is NULL
`df.dropna(how="all", subset=["order_id", "customer_id"])`, which drops a row only when both columns are NULL
`df.fillna({"order_id": 0, "customer_id": 0})`, which removes rows where either column is NULL

stem: Compliance requires that no record from the bronze `payments` table silently disappears when the silver table is built. About 2% of rows fail the rules (negative amount, unparseable date). Analysts want to see why each row failed and to reprocess fixed rows later. Which design meets this?

choices.text: Keep all rows in silver and replace invalid values with the column average so aggregates stay close to correct
Fail the whole job whenever any row is invalid and leave the entire bronze table unprocessed until the source is fixed
Filter the failing rows out of the silver load, then recover them from the bronze table's Delta time travel when needed
Write valid rows to silver, and write failing rows to a separate quarantine table with the reason for rejection

stem: A bronze column `price` holds text like `$1,234.50`. The silver table needs an exact numeric type for money, with two decimal places. Which expression produces it?

choices.text: `CAST(regexp_replace(price, '[$,]', '') AS DECIMAL(12,2))`
`CAST(regexp_replace(price, '[$,]', '') AS INT)`, which keeps the cents as a separate column automatically
`format_number(price, 2)`, which returns a numeric value with two decimals after removing the currency symbol
`CAST(price AS DOUBLE)`, which parses the dollar sign and thousands separator directly

stem: A silver `orders` table must keep every order, including orders whose customer id is missing from the `customers` dimension; for those orders the customer columns should be NULL. Which join achieves this?

choices.text: `orders o LEFT SEMI JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id`
`orders o LEFT JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id`
`orders o INNER JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id`
`orders o CROSS JOIN customers c`

stem: Data engineers need the list of orders whose `customer_id` has no row in the `customers` table, to send to the data steward. The result should contain only order columns. Which query does this most directly?

choices.text: `SELECT o.* FROM orders o INNER JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id <> c.customer_id`
`SELECT o.* FROM orders o LEFT SEMI JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id`
`SELECT o.* FROM orders o LEFT ANTI JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id`
`SELECT o.* FROM orders o FULL OUTER JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id`

stem: A silver job joins a 3 TB `transactions` table with a 4 MB `currency_codes` lookup table in PySpark. The team wants Spark to send the small table to all executors so that the large table is not shuffled across the network for this join. Which code expresses that intent?

choices.text: `from pyspark.sql.functions import broadcast; broadcast(tx).join(codes, "currency")`
`tx.repartition(2000, "currency").join(codes, "currency")`
`tx.join(codes.cache(), "currency")`
`from pyspark.sql.functions import broadcast; tx.join(broadcast(codes), "currency")`

stem: A join of `store_sales` to `store_prices` on `sku` alone produces about 10 times more rows than `store_sales` has. Each store sets its own price: `store_prices` has one row per (`store_id`, `sku`) pair. Sales totals are now overstated. What is the correct fix?

choices.text: Change the join condition to `s.store_id = p.store_id AND s.sku = p.sku` so each sale matches one price row
Switch from an inner join to a left join so unmatched rows no longer multiply, keeping the condition on `sku`
Use a CROSS JOIN with a WHERE clause on `sku` so Spark enumerates every price row before filtering
Add `DISTINCT` to the final SELECT list so duplicated rows collapse, keeping the join condition on `sku`

stem: A silver build joins `shipments` to `regions` with `ON s.region = r.region`. The `region` column is NULL in 5% of both tables, and the business wants NULL regions to be matched to NULL regions (both mean "unassigned"). Currently those shipments get no region data. Which condition fixes this?

choices.text: `coalesce(s.region, r.region) = r.region`, which sends NULL shipment regions to the region on the right table
`s.region = r.region OR s.region IS NULL`, which matches every shipment with a NULL region to every region row
`s.region == r.region`, which treats NULL values on both sides as equal in Spark
`s.region <=> r.region`, which is true when both sides are equal or both are NULL

stem: A reporting table needs one row per combination of the 300 active stores and the 12 months of the year, so that months without sales still show up with zero revenue after a later left join. Which operation creates the 3,600 combinations from a `stores` table and a `months` table?

choices.text: `stores CROSS JOIN months`
`stores LEFT SEMI JOIN months`
`stores FULL OUTER JOIN months ON stores.store_id = months.month_id`
`stores UNION ALL months`

stem: Two regional tables, `sales_emea` and `sales_apac`, have the same schema and hold distinct orders (an order never appears in both). A job appends the combined rows to a 900-million-row silver table every day. What is the best way to combine them?

choices.text: `SELECT * FROM sales_emea UNION SELECT * FROM sales_apac`, because UNION is the only operator that preserves duplicates
`SELECT * FROM sales_emea UNION ALL SELECT * FROM sales_apac`, because no duplicates between the tables exist to remove
`SELECT * FROM sales_emea EXCEPT SELECT * FROM sales_apac`, because EXCEPT keeps rows that appear in either table
`SELECT * FROM sales_emea INTERSECT SELECT * FROM sales_apac`, because INTERSECT combines both tables with the least data movement

stem: Two PySpark DataFrames have the same columns with the same types, but in different order: `df_a` is (`id`, `region`, `amount`) and `df_b` is (`id`, `amount`, `region`). The pipeline runs `df_a.union(df_b)`. The job succeeds, but `region` in the result sometimes contains numbers. What is the best fix?

choices.text: Use `df_a.join(df_b, "id", "outer")` because union cannot combine DataFrames with reordered columns
Use `df_a.union(df_b).distinct()` so the engine reconciles columns while deduplicating
Use `df_a.unionByName(df_b)` so the columns are matched by name instead of by position
Sort both DataFrames by `id` before the union so that Spark aligns the values correctly

stem: A new version of an upstream feed adds a column `channel` that older files do not have. The pipeline must combine the old DataFrame `df_old` (without `channel`) and the new DataFrame `df_new` (with `channel`), filling NULL for old rows. Which call does that?

choices.text: `df_old.unionByName(df_new, allowMissingColumns=True)`
`df_old.union(df_new)`, which pads the missing column with NULL automatically
`df_old.join(df_new, "id", "left_anti")`, which returns old rows with the new column added
`df_old.unionByName(df_new)`, which pads the missing column with NULL by default

stem: A PySpark join `orders.join(customers, orders.customer_id == customers.customer_id)` succeeds, but the next step `.select("customer_id")` fails with an ambiguous reference error because both DataFrames contribute a column with that name. Which change avoids the error and keeps a single `customer_id` column?

choices.text: `orders.join(customers, orders.customer_id == customers.customer_id, "cross")`
`orders.join(customers, on="customer_id")`, which merges the key into one output column
`orders.join(customers, orders.customer_id == customers.customer_id).dropDuplicates()`
`orders.join(customers, orders.customer_id == customers.customer_id).distinct("customer_id")`

stem: A bronze `orders` table has a column `items` of type `ARRAY<STRING>`. The silver table needs one row per order and item. Some orders have an empty array or a NULL array, and those orders must still appear once with a NULL item. Which expression does this?

choices.text: `SELECT order_id, size(items) AS item FROM bronze.orders`
`SELECT order_id, array_distinct(items) AS item FROM bronze.orders`
`SELECT order_id, explode_outer(items) AS item FROM bronze.orders`
`SELECT order_id, explode(items) AS item FROM bronze.orders`

stem: A table has an array column `steps` holding the ordered stages of a customer journey, for example `['visit','cart','buy']`. The silver table needs one row per stage together with its zero-based position in the array so the order can be restored. Which function is the most direct choice?

choices.text: `sort_array(steps)`, which returns each element with its position in a separate column
`array_position(steps, 'buy')`, which returns the position of each element in turn
`explode(steps)` followed by `row_number() OVER (ORDER BY step)`, which restores the original array order
`posexplode(steps)`, which returns both the position and the element for each array entry

stem: A silver job splits a pipe-delimited address column in PySpark with `F.split("addr", "|")`. Instead of `['12 Main St', 'Austin', 'TX']`, each row gets an array of single characters such as `['1','2',' ','M',...]`. What is the problem and the correct call?

choices.text: The second argument is a regular expression where `|` means alternation of empty patterns; use `F.split("addr", r"\|")`
`split` accepts only whitespace separators, so replace pipes with spaces first and split on `" "`
Separators must be a single quoted character, so use `F.split("addr", '"|"')` to pass it as a string
The limit argument defaults to 1, so use `F.split("addr", "|", -1)` to return all parts

stem: A large Delta table `silver.events` has a column `usr_id` that should be named `user_id` for all consumers. The team wants a metadata-only change that does not rewrite the data files. What should they do?

choices.text: Run `ALTER TABLE silver.events ADD COLUMN user_id` and copy the old values with a nightly job
Run `CREATE TABLE silver.events_new AS SELECT usr_id AS user_id, ... FROM silver.events`, then drop the old table
Run `df.withColumnRenamed("usr_id", "user_id")` in the notebook, which updates the column name stored in the table
Enable Delta column mapping on the table, then run `ALTER TABLE silver.events RENAME COLUMN usr_id TO user_id`

stem: A bronze `customers` table has 80 columns. The silver table must keep all of them except `ssn` and `birth_date`, and new columns added to bronze later should flow through automatically. The bronze table itself must stay untouched. Which query is the best fit?

choices.text: `ALTER TABLE bronze.customers DROP COLUMNS (ssn, birth_date)`
`SELECT * EXCEPT (ssn, birth_date) FROM bronze.customers`
`SELECT * FROM bronze.customers WHERE ssn IS NULL AND birth_date IS NULL`
`SELECT * FROM bronze.customers EXCEPT SELECT ssn, birth_date FROM bronze.customers`

stem: A bronze table has a STRUCT column `address` with fields `street`, `city` and `postal_code`. Silver should have these as three top-level columns next to `customer_id`, and new fields added to the struct later should appear automatically. Which query fits?

choices.text: `SELECT customer_id, split(address, '.') FROM bronze.customers`
`SELECT customer_id, explode(address) FROM bronze.customers`
`SELECT customer_id, address.* FROM bronze.customers`

Raise `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` to 2000 so that the collected data is spread across many more driver partitions in memory
Raise `spark.executor.memory` in the cluster Spark config so the workers can hold the collected rows
Add more worker nodes of the same type, because collected rows are then stored across the workers

stem: A transformation on a classic job cluster spills a lot of shuffle data to local disk because each executor has too little memory per core. An engineer proposes adding `spark.executor.memory 28g` to the job's Spark config. Another suggests following the Databricks compute best practices. What should the team do?

choices.text: Hardcode `spark.executor.memory` for every job, because Databricks recommends setting it explicitly to override its built-in sizing
Choose a memory-optimized worker instance type and avoid hardcoding `spark.executor.memory`
Set `spark.driver.memory` to a higher value, since spill is controlled by the driver heap rather than by executors
Disable adaptive query execution, because AQE is the reason that executors spill to local disk

stem: A job takes 40 minutes. After changing `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` from 200 to 2000, one run finishes in 31 minutes, and the engineer wants to roll the setting out to all jobs. The input volume of that run was lower than usual. What should the engineer do before concluding the change helped?

choices.text: Compare the run durations of two different days, since the input size has no effect on the run time of a Spark job
Treat the 31-minute run as proof and also raise the executor memory, since more changes give better results
Re-run both settings on the same input, changing only one at a time, and compare stage times and spill in the Spark UI
Apply the new setting to all jobs immediately, because any run that finishes faster proves that a higher partition count is better

stem: A gold layer must offer a regional sales summary built from a join and an aggregation over silver tables with hundreds of millions of rows. Fifty analysts open a dashboard on it all day, and the data only needs to be refreshed after each nightly load. Recomputing the query for every dashboard click is too slow and expensive. Which gold object fits?

choices.text: A standard view over the query, which stores the result of the first execution for later queries
A materialized view, which stores the query result and is refreshed after the source tables change
A streaming table that reads the silver tables and recomputes the summary again on each dashboard request
A temporary view in the analysts' notebooks, which Unity Catalog shares with all other users

stem: A retail company keeps a silver table of order lines and a customer dimension. A gold table must show revenue per customer segment. Customers are reassigned to new segments every week, and the figures must always reflect the current segment of each customer, including for past orders. Which gold object keeps the join correct?

choices.text: A standard view, because only a view can store both the join and its results at the same time
A streaming table, with a full refresh avoided, because stream joins are always correct without any reprocessing
A streaming table over the join, because it re-reads previous rows whenever the dimension changes
A materialized view over the join, because it recomputes affected results when the dimension changes

stem: Raw clickstream events (append-only, high volume) land continuously in a silver streaming table. A gold dataset must hold one enriched row per event, with a few derived columns computed from that row only. Each event must be processed exactly once as it arrives, with low latency, and rows that are already processed must not be recomputed. Which gold object fits?

choices.text: A streaming table that reads the silver table and applies the row-level transformations
A temporary table that is created at the start of each notebook session
A standard view that is queried by the dashboards when the data is needed
A materialized view, which is built to keep an aggregate or join result correct as the source data changes

stem: Auditors need a gold object that exposes only the columns `order_id`, `order_date` and `total` of a silver `orders` table with 60 other columns. It must always show current silver data, needs no extra storage or refresh schedule, and the query is cheap. Which object do you create?

choices.text: A view that selects the three columns from the silver table
A streaming table that appends the three columns for each new order only once
A deep clone of the silver table, with the other 60 columns dropped by hand
A materialized view that stores a copy of the three columns and is refreshed every night

stem: A gold table `customer_360` is maintained by a Lakeflow Jobs task that must apply updates from several upstream systems with custom `MERGE INTO` logic, delete rows on request, and be written by more than one job. BI tools only read it. Which gold object is appropriate?

choices.text: A streaming table, because several separate pipelines can write to a streaming table at the same time
A Delta table that jobs write with `MERGE INTO`, because jobs control its writes directly
A materialized view, because jobs can run `MERGE INTO` and `DELETE` statements on it directly
A standard view, because a view accepts `MERGE INTO` and routes the changes to the silver tables

stem: A gold materialized view `daily_revenue` is queried by dashboards. After the nightly silver load finished at 02:00, analysts still see yesterday's numbers at 08:00. The view was created without a refresh schedule. Which action brings it up to date and prevents the problem in future?

choices.text: Run `INSERT INTO daily_revenue SELECT ...` for the missing day, because materialized views accept inserts like tables
Run `VACUUM daily_revenue`, because vacuum recomputes stored query results from the source tables
Drop the silver tables and recreate them, because a materialized view refreshes only when its source tables are recreated
Run `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW daily_revenue` now, and add a `SCHEDULE` clause or run the refresh as a task after the silver load

stem: A Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines silver streaming table `clean_orders` must not contain rows where `order_id` is NULL. The team wants those rows removed from the target automatically, and the number of dropped rows visible as a data quality metric. The pipeline must keep running. Which declaration fits?

choices.text: `CONSTRAINT valid_order_id EXPECT (order_id IS NOT NULL) ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE`
`CONSTRAINT valid_order_id CHECK (order_id IS NOT NULL)` added with `ALTER TABLE` after the pipeline run
`CONSTRAINT valid_order_id EXPECT (order_id IS NOT NULL) ON VIOLATION DROP ROW`
`CONSTRAINT valid_order_id EXPECT (order_id IS NOT NULL)` with no violation action

stem: In a gold materialized view of a Lakeflow pipeline, any negative `revenue` value means that a broken upstream calculation ran, and finance does not want a partial or wrong report published. The refresh must stop and leave the previous good result untouched. Which expectation action is correct?

choices.text: The default `EXPECT` with no action, which records metrics and writes the invalid rows to the view
`ON VIOLATION DROP ROW`, which removes negative rows so that the rest of the data is published
`ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE`, which makes the update fail and prevents invalid records from being published
A temporary view with a comment documenting the rule, which Databricks enforces during refresh

stem: A team runs `ALTER TABLE main.silver.payments ADD CONSTRAINT positive_amount CHECK (amount > 0)` on a Delta table that has been in production for a year. The statement fails. Which is the most likely cause and the correct next step?

choices.text: The constraint name `positive_amount` is reserved by Unity Catalog, so a different name will make it succeed
CHECK constraints are informational only, so the statement fails until the table is registered as external
CHECK constraints cannot be added after table creation, so the table must be recreated with the constraint
Some existing rows have `amount <= 0`; fix or remove those rows, then add the constraint

stem: A silver table is created with `id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, name STRING` in Unity Catalog. A job later inserts two rows with the same `id`, and the insert succeeds. The engineer expected an error. Why did it succeed?

choices.text: Primary key constraints on Databricks are informational and not enforced; only NOT NULL and CHECK are enforced
The insert bypassed the constraint because serverless compute never evaluates Delta constraints
Unity Catalog enforces primary keys only at read time, so the duplicate appears only when someone queries it
Primary keys are enforced only when the table is partitioned by the key column, which this table is not

stem: A silver streaming table in a Lakeflow pipeline must reject orders whose `customer_id` does not exist in the `customers` table. An engineer writes `EXPECT (customer_id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM customers))` and the pipeline fails validation. What is the correct approach?

choices.text: Replace the subquery with a custom Python UDF that looks up the customers table for each record
Subqueries on other tables are not allowed in expectations, so join with `customers` in the query and test the result
Move the rule to an external REST service that the expectation calls for each record
Use a `NOT NULL` constraint on `customer_id`, because it also checks that the value exists in the customers table

stem: A silver streaming table in a Lakeflow pipeline receives payments, and about 1% fail the rule `amount > 0 AND currency IS NOT NULL`. Compliance wants valid rows in `payments_clean` and the invalid rows kept in a separate table for review, with no row lost and no pipeline failure. Which design fits?

choices.text: Define the rule once, load valid rows with an expect-or-drop expectation and invalid rows into a second table using the negated rule
Put an expect-or-drop expectation on `payments_clean` only, because dropped rows are stored automatically in a hidden review table
Use the default warn expectation on `payments_clean` and tell reviewers to filter invalid rows out of it in every dashboard
Use a fail-update expectation on `payments_clean` so that invalid rows stop the pipeline and are saved inside the failure message

stem: A nightly join-and-aggregate job has one stage that runs for 40 minutes while the rest finish in minutes. On the stage page in the Spark UI, the Summary Metrics table shows a median task duration of 20 seconds, a 75th percentile of 25 seconds and a maximum of 38 minutes. The cluster has 64 cores and most of them sit idle during the last minutes of the stage. What does this pattern indicate?

choices.text: A cold disk cache: the first reads of the stage were slow, which lifts the maximum duration without affecting the 75th percentile
Too many shuffle partitions: the tiny median task time proves that Spark created more tasks than the stage needed
Data skew: a few tasks process far more data than the others, so the cores that finish early wait for the long tasks
Disk spill: every task ran out of execution memory and wrote its data to local disk before the stage could finish

stem: A join-heavy batch ETL job is slow. The stage page of the longest stage shows spill statistics (data written from memory to disk), and task durations are similar across the stage, so there is no skew. The workers are many small instances. Which change addresses the cause most directly?

choices.text: Enable the disk cache on the workers, because a cache holds shuffle data in memory and removes the need to spill
Increase the number of workers while keeping the same small instance type, so more tasks run in parallel on identical memory
Cast every column to STRING before the join, so Spark can use a simpler row format with a smaller memory footprint
Use fewer, larger worker instances with more memory, so more shuffle data fits in execution memory before it must be written to disk

stem: A batch job reads a large Delta table with a selective filter on `store_id`. The longest stage in the Spark UI shows a very large Input column and almost no shuffle or output, there is no skew or spill, and throughput per core is around 3 MB per second. The table has no clustering. What should the engineer do to cut the stage time?

choices.text: Add a `REBALANCE` hint to the query so that Spark splits oversized output partitions evenly
Cluster the table on `store_id` with liquid clustering so that data skipping lets the stage read far fewer files
Increase the executor memory so that the input data stays in memory instead of spilling to disk
Raise `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` to 2000 so that the large input is divided among more shuffle tasks

stem: A shuffle-heavy aggregation stage reads 900 GB of shuffle data, and the stage page shows the Shuffle Read column as the largest I/O value. Task times are even and there is no spill. The team set `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` to 200 years ago and never revisited it, and input sizes now change a lot from run to run. Which setting does Databricks recommend to reduce the shuffle time?

choices.text: Set `spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold` to -1 so that every aggregation avoids the shuffle by broadcasting its input
Set `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` to `auto` so that Spark picks the number of shuffle partitions from the query plan and input data size
Set `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` to 1 so that no data has to be exchanged between executors during the aggregation
Set `spark.sql.adaptive.enabled` to false so that the plan is fixed and the same number of partitions is used on every run

stem: A sort merge join stage shows skew: the maximum task duration is many times the 75th percentile. Adaptive query execution is on, yet the skewed partitions, about 150 MB each, are not being split. A colleague notes the skewed partitions are smaller than the AQE skew thresholds. Which action fits?

choices.text: Turn AQE off and set the shuffle partitions to 1, because Spark then no longer compares partition sizes with thresholds
Add a broadcast hint on the large side of the join, because AQE splits skewed partitions of broadcast joins first
Lower `spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.skewedPartitionThresholdInBytes` (and the factor if needed) so AQE treats these partitions as skewed
Increase `spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.skewedPartitionThresholdInBytes` so that more partitions qualify as skewed

stem: A 5 TB events table is clustered with `CLUSTER BY (customer_id)`. Analysts now filter mostly on `event_date` and `country`, so the team runs `ALTER TABLE events CLUSTER BY (event_date, country)`. The command finishes immediately, but queries on the new keys are still slow for old data. What explains this and what is the next step?

choices.text: Clustering keys are applied by `VACUUM`, so run `VACUUM events` to rewrite the old files with the new layout
The table must be dropped and recreated, because clustering keys of a Delta table cannot be changed after creation
Old data is reclustered by the next `OPTIMIZE events ZORDER BY (event_date, country)`, which replaces the clustering keys
Changing keys only affects newly written data; run `OPTIMIZE events FULL` to recluster the existing files with the new keys

stem: A catalog has predictive optimization enabled, but a team's `clicks` table never gets compaction or statistics maintenance even after months. DESCRIBE EXTENDED shows the table is an external Delta table in the team's own S3 bucket. What explains this, and what is the durable fix?

choices.text: Predictive optimization runs only on Unity Catalog managed tables, so convert the table to a managed table
Predictive optimization only maintains Iceberg tables, so the team must rewrite the table in the Iceberg format
Predictive optimization skips tables above a certain data size, so the team must split the table into smaller tables
Predictive optimization needs a Python notebook that calls `OPTIMIZE` once, so the team must add one to a job

stem: A data engineer wants Databricks to choose and adapt the clustering keys of a Unity Catalog managed table from its query history, instead of fixing keys by hand. Which statement does this?

choices.text: `ALTER TABLE sales SET MANAGED`
`ALTER TABLE sales SET TBLPROPERTIES ('delta.autoOptimize.optimizeWrite' = 'true')`
`ALTER TABLE sales CLUSTER BY AUTO`
`ALTER TABLE sales CLUSTER BY NONE`

stem: A schema contains managed tables with predictive optimization enabled through the catalog. A nightly Lakeflow Jobs task still runs `OPTIMIZE` on each liquid-clustered table in that schema, and the team asks if it is still needed. Which decision is best?

choices.text: Remove the scheduled OPTIMIZE task, because predictive optimization runs OPTIMIZE for enabled tables automatically
Replace the task with `OPTIMIZE ... ZORDER BY`, because predictive optimization performs Z-ordering on clustered tables
Keep the task and add a nightly VACUUM as well, because predictive optimization only maintains statistics
Keep the task, because predictive optimization can run only when the scheduled task is paused

stem: Predictive optimization is enabled for the catalog `prod`. The schema `prod.scratch` holds short-lived tables that are rewritten every hour, and the team does not want any maintenance compute spent on them, while all other schemas should stay enabled. Which statement fits?

choices.text: `ALTER SCHEMA prod.scratch INHERIT PREDICTIVE OPTIMIZATION`
`ALTER SCHEMA prod.scratch DISABLE PREDICTIVE OPTIMIZATION`
`ALTER CATALOG prod DISABLE PREDICTIVE OPTIMIZATION`
`ALTER TABLE prod.scratch.* DISABLE PREDICTIVE OPTIMIZATION`

stem: After a Delta pipeline team added a cluster-scoped init script that installs an OS package, every start of their classic cluster fails during launch. The script ends with a failing command, and the cluster event log shows an init script failure. What is the most effective way to find the cause?

choices.text: Increase the driver node size, because init scripts that exceed driver memory terminate the cluster launch
Switch the cluster to serverless compute for notebooks, which runs the same init script with less memory pressure
Move the script to a global init script, because global scripts ignore non-zero exit codes during startup
Configure cluster log delivery and read the init script log, because a non-zero exit code of the script fails the launch

stem: Right after a new AWS-based workspace was deployed into the customer's own VPC, the first classic cluster never becomes ready. After roughly 30 minutes the event log reports that the compute plane network is misconfigured and that the node daemon ping timed out. What should the engineer check first?

choices.text: The Spark configuration `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions`, because a wrong value stops nodes from joining the cluster
The library list of the cluster, because a missing PyPI package prevents the node daemon from answering pings
The Delta table properties of the tables that the first notebook reads, since a wrong property can stop the bootstrap of nodes
Routing and firewall rules, to confirm the instances can reach the Databricks control plane, for example with `nc -zv` tests

stem: A notebook on a classic cluster has already run `import pandas` in an earlier cell. Cell 1 then upgrades the library with `%pip install --upgrade pandas`, and in cell 2 `pandas.__version__` still prints the old version, although the install log reports success. What is the cause and the fix?

choices.text: `%pip` installs only on the driver of another cluster, so the library must be added through the Jobs API
Libraries from PyPI always lose to the copy in Databricks Runtime, so the only option is to upload the wheel file to DBFS
`%pip` does not restart the Python process; call `dbutils.library.restartPython()` so the notebook imports the new version
The install only applies to the next cluster start, so the cluster must be terminated and started again

stem: A notebook reads a 400 GB Delta table into a DataFrame and calls `rows = df.collect()` to loop over the rows in Python. The run fails with an out-of-memory error on the driver, while the executors show low memory use. What is the best fix?

choices.text: Keep the work distributed: use DataFrame or SQL transformations and write the result to a table instead of collecting rows
Call `df.cache()` first, because a cached DataFrame is returned to the driver in compressed form with no extra memory use
Increase `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions`, because the rows collected are limited by the number of shuffle partitions
Add more worker nodes, because executor memory is where `collect()` stores the returned rows

stem: A team registers `raw_events` as an external Unity Catalog table on `s3://acme-landing/events/`, which a partner process also reads. A cleanup script now runs `DROP TABLE main.landing.raw_events`. What happens to the files in the bucket?

choices.text: Unity Catalog deletes the files immediately, because every dropped table has its data removed from storage
Unity Catalog removes only the table metadata, and the data files stay in cloud storage until someone deletes them
Unity Catalog deletes the files only after the 7-day default recovery period, because external tables use it as well
Unity Catalog moves the files into the schema's managed storage location and keeps them for the recovery period

stem: A Delta table `main.sales.orders_ext` is an external Unity Catalog table, owned by the engineer, in an S3 location. The team wants it managed by Unity Catalog, keeping its name, permissions and history, with minimal downtime for readers and writers. Which statement should the engineer run, on a runtime that supports it?

choices.text: `ALTER TABLE main.sales.orders_ext SET MANAGED`
`CREATE TABLE main.sales.orders_mgd AS SELECT * FROM main.sales.orders_ext`
`ALTER TABLE main.sales.orders_ext SET MANAGED MOVE`
`ALTER TABLE main.sales.orders_ext UNSET MANAGED`

stem: Ten days after converting an external Delta table to managed with `SET MANAGED`, the team finds that a partner tool needs the original external location again. They want the table back as external while keeping the writes made since the conversion. What should they do?

choices.text: Drop the managed table and re-create the external table by hand from the old location with `CREATE TABLE ... LOCATION`
Run `ALTER TABLE ... UNSET MANAGED` within the 14-day rollback window, before dropping the managed table
Run `UNDROP TABLE` on the managed table, because it restores the pre-conversion external location
Run `ALTER TABLE ... SET EXTERNAL` for a new bucket, because rollback is not possible after any writes

stem: A data engineer who has `USE CATALOG`, `USE SCHEMA` and `CREATE TABLE` on `main.finance` runs `CREATE TABLE main.finance.audit_ext (id BIGINT) LOCATION 's3://acme-finance/audit/'`. The statement fails with a permission error. Which missing privilege explains it?

choices.text: `SELECT` on the metastore, which allows queries of any table in it
`CREATE MANAGED STORAGE` on the catalog `main`, which sets where its managed tables are stored
`MODIFY` on the schema `main.finance`
`CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE` on the external location covering `s3://acme-finance/audit/`

stem: A team has a feed of Avro files that must be registered as a queryable table in Unity Catalog, and another non-Databricks application reads the same files directly from the bucket. Which table type fits?

choices.text: A managed table, because managed tables accept Avro files as their storage format
A managed table, because other tools can then read the files directly with no restrictions on path-based access
An external table, because it can register data in file formats such as Avro and leaves the files in the bucket
A foreign table, because it registers files in cloud storage with the same governance as an external table

stem: An engineer inherits several tables in `main.ops` and needs to know for each whether it is managed or external and where its files live, using SQL only. Which command shows this?

choices.text: `SHOW TABLES IN main.ops`, which lists the table type and storage location of every table in the schema
`SHOW GRANTS ON TABLE main.ops.shipments`, which lists the table type and the storage location of the data files
`DESCRIBE EXTENDED main.ops.shipments`, which lists the table type and the storage location among the details
`DESCRIBE HISTORY main.ops.shipments`, which lists the table type and storage location from the transaction log

stem: Last week an engineer ran `DROP TABLE main.sales.daily_totals` on a Unity Catalog managed table by mistake. Nobody changed the catalog's retention settings. The table is needed again today with its data. What is the right action?

choices.text: Re-create the table with `CREATE TABLE` and re-ingest everything, because dropped managed tables are purged immediately
Run `UNDROP TABLE main.sales.daily_totals`, because dropped managed tables remain recoverable for a default period of 7 days
Run `RESTORE TABLE main.sales.daily_totals TO VERSION AS OF 0`, because RESTORE works on tables that no longer exist
Run `REFRESH TABLE main.sales.daily_totals`, because it re-registers a dropped table from its storage files

stem: A BI group `analysts` must query only `main.sales.orders` and nothing else. The group has no privileges yet. Which set of grants is sufficient and follows least privilege?

choices.text: `SELECT` on the catalog `main`, because catalog-level grants are required for any table query
`SELECT` on `main.sales.orders` alone, because table privileges include access to the parents
`USE CATALOG` on `main` and `SELECT` on `main.sales`, because schema-level grants pass access up to the catalog
`USE CATALOG` on `main`, `USE SCHEMA` on `main.sales` and `SELECT` on `main.sales.orders`

stem: Data scientists in the group `ds_team` need `SELECT` on every table in `main.features`, including tables created there in the future, without anyone running new grants. They already hold `USE CATALOG` on `main` and `USE SCHEMA` on the schema. Which grant fits?

choices.text: `GRANT SELECT ON SCHEMA main.features TO ds_team`
`GRANT SELECT ON TABLE main.features.* TO ds_team`
`GRANT SELECT ON CATALOG main TO ds_team`
`GRANT USE SCHEMA ON SCHEMA main.features TO ds_team`

stem: A Lakeflow Jobs pipeline runs as the service principal with application ID `5f2c8a1e-0000-4d11-9b7e-aaaabbbbcccc`. It must read and append rows to existing tables in `main.etl`. It already has `USE CATALOG` and `USE SCHEMA`. Which statement grants what is missing?

choices.text: `GRANT MANAGE ON SCHEMA main.etl TO `5f2c8a1e-0000-4d11-9b7e-aaaabbbbcccc``
`GRANT SELECT, MODIFY ON SCHEMA main.etl TO `5f2c8a1e-0000-4d11-9b7e-aaaabbbbcccc``
`GRANT SELECT ON SCHEMA main.etl TO `5f2c8a1e-0000-4d11-9b7e-aaaabbbbcccc``
`GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON CATALOG main TO `5f2c8a1e-0000-4d11-9b7e-aaaabbbbcccc``

stem: To keep contractors out of HR data in a Unity Catalog metastore, an engineer runs `DENY SELECT ON TABLE main.hr.salaries TO contractors`. What should the engineer expect?

choices.text: The statement succeeds but only for users who are not metastore admins, because admins bypass the deny
The statement succeeds, and the deny is inherited by `main.hr` schema and every other table in it
The statement blocks the group even if the group holds a `SELECT` grant on the schema, because a deny takes precedence in Unity Catalog
`DENY` applies only to the legacy `hive_metastore` catalog; in Unity Catalog, access is controlled by not granting or by revoking

stem: The group `interns` received `SELECT` on the catalog `main`. A manager wants interns to lose access to all tables of `main.finance` but keep access to the rest of `main`. An admin runs `REVOKE SELECT ON TABLE main.finance.payroll FROM interns` and finds that interns can still query `payroll`. Why, and what fits the requirement?

choices.text: Revoking at table level only removes metadata access, so the interns still read the data until their compute restarts
Unity Catalog caches grants for 24 hours, so the revoke takes effect on the next day with no other change
The grant is on the catalog and inherited by the table, so revoke it there and re-grant `SELECT` on the schemas interns keep
The revoke must be repeated for each user in the group, because a group member's access is stored per user

stem: A senior engineer is the owner of the schema `main.curated`, but does not own the table `main.curated.invoices`, which was created by a colleague. The engineer needs to give the group `finance_ro` access to read that table. Which statement is true?

choices.text: The engineer can grant it, because the owner of the containing schema may grant privileges on the table
The engineer cannot grant it, because only account admins can grant privileges on tables
The engineer cannot grant it, because only the owner of the table itself may grant privileges on that table
The engineer can grant it, but only after being given `ALL PRIVILEGES` on the table

stem: The group `platform_team` was given `GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON SCHEMA main.shared TO platform_team`. Members can read, write and create tables there, but an attempt to run `GRANT SELECT ON SCHEMA main.shared TO partners` fails for them. What explains it?

choices.text: `ALL PRIVILEGES` does not include `MANAGE`, so the team cannot manage privileges on the schema until it is granted `MANAGE` or ownership
`ALL PRIVILEGES` covers only data privileges at table level, so a schema-level grant never lets the team create tables
The statement fails because a schema can be shared with one group at a time, so `partners` must be removed from other schemas first
Groups cannot hold grant rights, because only individual users can manage privileges in Unity Catalog
